Uncouth

un-KOOTH · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Uncouth is lacking proper manners, refinement, or social grace.

Putting his feet up on the desk during the job interview struck the hiring manager as deeply uncouth.

Worked Example

Wiping his hands on the tablecloth instead of his napkin, the guest seemed blissfully unaware of how uncouth his table manners really were.

Uncouth describes specific behaviors -- table manners, grooming, speech -- that fall short of what's socially expected, rather than a person's whole personality.

How Uncouth Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

crude

crude: lacking refinement or tact

coarse

coarse: rough or unrefined in manner

Antonyms

refined

refined: elegant and polished in manner

polite

polite: showing good manners and consideration

How Strong Is It? — crude → uncouth → boorish

crude vs. uncouth

crude vs. uncouth: Crude is a bit milder -- it can describe rough humor or unpolished work, not just bad manners.

boorish vs. uncouth

boorish vs. uncouth: Boorish (from this unit's own boor) goes further, describing someone whose lack of manners makes them genuinely unpleasant company.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of uncouth.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — un-

prefix — un-: not (Old English un-)

root — -couth

root — -couth: known, familiar (i.e., familiar with proper manners) (Old English cuð)

Put it together

Put it together: Uncouth comes from Old English un- ('not') plus cuð ('known, familiar') -- someone uncouth is, literally, 'unfamiliar' with proper manners and polite behavior.

Use the root in a new word: couth

Use the root in a new word: couth: Couth is the rarer opposite of uncouth -- people sometimes jokingly say someone is 'quite couth' to mean they have excellent manners.
